<a name="dp-1"></a>

## 1. A recommendation without a citation is an opinion — make the citation structural

The premise of an anthology of current practice is that every entry has a
reason, and the reason is somebody's published work. That premise survives
exactly as long as the link from claim to evidence is mandatory. Make it
optional and it decays quietly: nothing breaks, the list still renders, and
over time it becomes a list of assertions with a provenance field that is
usually blank.

The mechanism is not "remember to cite". It is that a document which does not
name its source fails the build. In this record that is
`requires = ["source"]` on the `SOTA` scheme, and it is a small enough thing
that it is worth being precise about why it works: the check fires at the
moment of writing, while the person filing the practice still knows where
they read it. A citation reconstructed six months later costs a session; one
written at filing time costs a line.

Applied here: `SOTA` requires `source:`, `LIT` requires `arxiv:` — which
immediately found two papers in the corpus that had reached it with no
identifier at all. The arXiv remote turns those ids into resolvable
references rather than strings, so "cite the paper" and "the citation
resolves" are the same check rather than two.

The corollary is the expensive part. Requiring the field is easy; keeping it
*meaningful* means the evidence has to be a document in the record, not a
URL — because a URL cannot be found to be retired, cannot be counted, and
cannot tell you that eleven practices depend on a paper you just decided was
wrong.

*v1 · shaped by [ADR-001](../record/decisions.d/ADR-001.md), [ADR-002](../record/decisions.d/ADR-002.md) · origin: 119 recommendations carried a `source` field and not one carried the `supporting_evidence` the schema defined for it — the field existed, was empty in every record, and nothing noticed for two years*

<a name="dp-2"></a>

## 2. A field every record shares is not a field — it is a comment with a schema

When every record agrees, the field has told you nothing. The dangerous part
is that it does not *look* like nothing: it looks like a tracked attribute.
It has a type, it appears in the documentation, downstream code branches on
it. A reviewer reading the schema concludes the project distinguishes three
kinds of recommendation. A reviewer reading the data would have found it
distinguishes none.

The failure that produces this is almost never "nobody set the field". It is
that the code which *would* set it cannot run. Here, both branches that could
assign a non-default status read a list that no qualifying record had, so
they were unreachable on the actual corpus — and unreachable code fails
silently by construction, because the way it announces itself is by not
happening.

So the check has to be on the data, not on the code. "Do the records
disagree?" is answerable by looking at them and unanswerable by reading the
branch that was supposed to make them disagree.

Applied here: `luria lint` reports `inert-status` when every document in a
scheme shares one status, above a floor where uniformity stops being
explainable by youth. The `SOTA` scheme now holds 119 `Active` and one
`Deferred` — a thin margin, and an honest one, because the `Deferred` record
is the one hedge the corpus actually contained.

The corollary: a uniform field is not automatically a bug, and treating it as
one produces a check people switch off. Sometimes every record really is in
force. The finding is *"this field is currently carrying no information"*,
addressed to a person, and a scheme that declares a vocabulary of one is a
project saying so deliberately.

*v1 · shaped by [ADR-001](../record/decisions.d/ADR-001.md), [ADR-002](../record/decisions.d/ADR-002.md) · origin: All 119 recommendations sat at one status because the two code paths that could set any other read a field no qualifying paper had. The schema defined three states, the data expressed one, and the build was green throughout*

<a name="dp-3"></a>

## 3. Keep what you stopped believing — the contrast is most of the content

"Do this" is advice. "Do this, and here is the thing everybody did until 2021
and why it stopped being right" is knowledge. The second is what a reader
comes for, and it only exists if the abandoned position is still written
down.

There is a sharper reason than pedagogy. A document that silently drops what
it used to say cannot be checked. Every version of it looks equally
authoritative, because the evidence of it having been wrong is removed at the
same time as the wrongness. This is the specific way a "living document" goes
bad: not by being wrong, but by becoming unable to be shown to have been.

Retirement therefore has to be an edit to a status, never a deletion — and
the reason has to render where a reader meets the entry, not sit in a field
that only the file's author ever opens.

Applied here: `Rejected` and `Superseded` are statuses on a document that
keeps its body; retired entries appear in the generated index with their
reason in the status column; and a live practice citing a retired paper is a
lint finding rather than something to be noticed. The migration surfaced a
chain nobody could have read from the source data — a paper superseded by one
that was itself later rejected — which is exactly the shape of thing that
only exists if you kept both.

The corollary people skip: keeping the entry obliges you to keep it
*findable*. A retired document that stays in the record but drops out of the
indexes has been deleted in every sense that matters to a reader; it just
still occupies a file.

*v1 · shaped by [ADR-004](../record/decisions.d/ADR-004.md) · origin: Nine papers had been retired with reasons good enough to be worth reading — "too domain-specific", "needs per-case tuning, no consistent benefit" — and every one of those reasons was invisible in generated output*
